strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: diversity collapse ('reward hacking') in RL post-training for real-time music accompaniment, a setting where the failure mode directly harms human-AI interaction quality.

Method is clearly presented: GAIL/AMP-style discriminator reward added to a PPO pipeline, with a sensible two-phase (warmup + confidence-gated) discriminator update schedule to handle reward nonstationarity, formalized in Algorithm 1.

Well-designed ablation: 'GAPT w/o Adv. Training' keeps all other components identical, so the causal contribution of the adversarial reward is cleanly isolated and consistently shows restored diversity with no loss of harmony (Tables 1-2, Figures 4 and 6).

Unusually broad evaluation for this area: fixed-melody simulation, out-of-distribution evaluation (Wikifonia), learned melody-agent co-adaptation, perturbation/recovery analysis (Figure 7), and an IRB-approved user study with 12 expert musicians including qualitative feedback that directly illustrates the targeted tradeoff.
Good reproducibility commitments: release of training datasets, model checkpoints, code, plus detailed architecture/hyperparameter descriptions and reward-model test-set performance in the appendix.
Honest and nuanced discussion, e.g., acknowledging that Online MLE appears strongest in model-model co-adaptation and explaining why this does not transfer to human partners.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea (discriminator-derived adversarial reward during policy training, à la GAIL/AIRL/AMP) is well established; the two-phase adaptive update schedule is heuristic engineering rather than a principled algorithmic contribution, and no theoretical analysis of why the schedule works is provided.

Potential circularity in diversity evaluation: the Vendi Score and t-SNE embeddings are computed using the chord encoder from the contrastive coherence reward model, which is also part of the training reward ensemble. The adversarial reward pushes policy outputs toward data in learned-embedding space, so 'higher diversity' on this metric may partly reflect the shared representation rather than perceptual diversity; no independent or human-judged diversity measure is provided.

Baseline fairness concern: the reproduced ReaLchords baseline is trained only on Hooktheory while GAPT and the ablation are trained on three datasets, confounding the head-to-head comparison against the prior published system.

User study is modest: N=12, only three single-item Likert questions, significance (p<0.05) reported for only two of three items, and no discussion of multiple-comparison correction or effect sizes; 'harmony diversity' of live user sessions relies on the same circular embedding metric.

Missing ablations on the method's own hyperparameters: sensitivity to the confidence gate threshold (τ=1.0), warmup length, discriminator capacity, and label smoothing are not explored; the two-phase schedule itself is not compared against simpler alternatives (e.g., fixed-ratio updates throughout, or gradient-based balancing).

Absolute harmony levels are far below ground truth (0.497 vs 0.727 note-in-chord ratio), and the note-in-chord metric is crude (ignores voice-leading, chord extensions, timing); the musical validity of the gains is ultimately supported only by the small user study.

The melody jamming agent used in co-adaptation evaluation is itself trained with the adversarial reward, which could favor the adversarially trained chord policy and partially confound the model-model comparison.

strengths: The problem setting — real-time, live human-AI music jamming under an online constraint (Eq. 2) that forbids access to the partner's future moves — is genuinely challenging, well-motivated, and underexplored; the paper clearly articulates why diversity collapse from coherence-only RL rewards is particularly harmful here.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this domain: three progressive interactivity settings (fixed-melody simulation, model–model co-adaptation, live user study), out-of-distribution evaluation (Wikifonia), perturbation/recovery analysis (Fig. 7), and an IRB-approved user study with 12 expert musicians including qualitative feedback.

The paper is transparent about negative behaviors (repetitive accompaniment under ReaLchords), includes an ablation (GAPT w/o Adv.), and commits to releasing datasets, checkpoints, training infrastructure, and the real-time interactive system, which supports reproducibility.

The diagnosis of diversity collapse as reward hacking, and the framing of the discriminator as a complementary constraint to the coherence reward (hacked repetitive outputs get low realism; realism-chasing outputs get low coherence), is intuitively appealing and pedagogically clear.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty. The core method is a GAIL-style discriminator reward (Ho & Ermon, 2016) added to PPO, plus label smoothing and a heuristic two-phase/adaptive discriminator update schedule (fixed interval, then a moving-average threshold gate). All of these components are standard or hand-tuned heuristics; the paper itself concedes adversarial rewards 'have fallen out of favor' and mostly re-applies a known technique to a new domain. This is an application paper, not a methodological contribution commensurate with a top-tier AI venue.

Confounded baseline comparison. The ReaLchords reproduction is trained only on the Hooktheory dataset, while GAPT is trained on three datasets (Hooktheory, POP909, Nottingham) with different sampling probabilities. The headline claim that GAPT outperforms ReaLchords on diversity and harmony therefore confounds the adversarial-reward method with substantially more training data. The 'GAPT w/o Adv.' ablation mitigates this partially, but the primary baseline comparison in Table 1/2 is not apples-to-apples.

The diversity metric is circular. The Vendi Score is computed using embeddings from the contrastive reward model — the very model whose reward the policy was trained to maximize. A policy optimized (even partially) against this encoder may score higher on diversity measured in that encoder's space without a corresponding perceptual or ground-truth diversity gain. No independent diversity metric (e.g., n-gram chord coverage, human-rated variety) validates the claim.

The central claim that 'the KL constraint is insufficient to mitigate reward hacking' (a key positioning argument vs. standard practice) is asserted but never experimentally demonstrated: there is no KL-regularized PPO ablation with a swept β, no elastic-reset or reward-shaping baseline despite these being cited as the main alternatives. GAPT w/o Adv. does include a KL term, but the KL-vs-adversarial comparison the narrative depends on is missing.

Evaluation gaps and modest effects. Note-in-chord ratio is a crude harmony proxy; all systems fall far below ground truth (0.50 vs 0.73 on test), so 'harmonic coherence' gains are relative to a weak frontier. Diversity improvements over the ablation are modest (26.6 vs 20.8 on test; 11.3 vs 8.0 OOD), and the user study (N=12, three 5-point Likert items) yields significance only on two of three items versus one baseline; no correction for multiple comparisons is reported.

The discriminator sees only the chord sequence y, not the interaction (x, y) pair. Realism is thus an input-agnostic prior on chords alone, which weakens the mechanistic story about 'reward hacking of the coherence reward' — the discriminator cannot detect melodic incoherence, and the claimed complementary-pressure argument is only half-instantiated.

Scale and generality are limited: small models (8-layer, hidden dim 512), symbolic melody-to-chords only, monophonic lead-follow setting with a fixed melody agent; the abstract and conclusion generalize to 'RL post-training of generative sequence models,' but there is no evidence (e.g., text or other sequence domains) that the finding transfers beyond this narrow task.

Stability of the two-phase schedule is asserted, not shown: no training curves of the adversarial reward, no comparison against a naive joint-update baseline or alternative gates (τ, window, warmup are single-point choices), so the 'stabilizing' contribution of the schedule is unsupported.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: reward hacking / diversity collapse in RL post-training of generative sequence models, studied in a genuinely challenging real-time interactive setting.

The proposed GAPT method is well-motivated and technically reasonable: it combines a GAIL-style adversarial reward with a coherence reward, and the two-phase, confidence-gated discriminator update schedule is a practical contribution for stabilizing the nonstationary adversarial signal.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: three progressively interactive settings (fixed-melody simulation, model-model co-adaptation, and a real-time user study with 12 expert musicians), an out-of-distribution dataset, an input-perturbation robustness experiment, an ablation isolating the adversarial reward, and IRB-approved human study procedures with both quantitative ratings and qualitative feedback.

The paper is transparent about limitations of pure coherence-only RL and carefully contrasts the adversarial approach with KL-based regularization, arguing (and showing evidence) that KL alone is insufficient in this setting.

Strong reproducibility commitments: datasets, checkpoints, training infrastructure, and the real-time interactive system are released, and hyperparameters and architecture details are reported in the appendix.
The user study results (significantly higher adaptation speed and perceived agency, p < 0.05) together with qualitative comments align well with the simulation findings, supporting the central claim.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty. The core mechanism is a standard GAIL-style discriminator reward (Ho & Ermon, 2016) applied on top of an existing system (ReaLchords); similar adversarial reward-model training already exists for mitigating reward hacking (Bukharin et al., 2025) and for motion naturalness (AMP, Peng et al., 2021). The two-phase schedule is heuristic rather than principled, and its hyperparameters (τ=1.0, K_int=5, m=3, α=0.1) are fixed without sensitivity analysis.

Potential circularity in evaluation: both the diversity metric (Vendi Score) and the t-SNE visualization use the chord encoder from the contrastive reward model, and the note-in-chord harmony metric is closely related to the coherence reward family. A policy optimized with adversarial/coherence rewards may partially game these metrics, so reported gains on the Pareto frontier should be interpreted cautiously.

Quantitative gains are modest and not uniformly dominant: on the out-of-distribution dataset, GAPT's harmony (0.470) is slightly below ReaLchords (0.475), and GAPT's diversity (26.645) remains below Online MLE (29.491) and Ground Truth (27.922). Tables 1 and 2 report no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple training seeds, so it is unclear whether the differences are statistically reliable.

Baseline comparison confound: the reproduced ReaLchords baseline is trained only on the Hooktheory dataset while GAPT is trained on three datasets, and GAPT adds an entropy term that ReaLchords lacks; although the GAPT w/o Adv ablation isolates the adversarial reward, the headline comparison against ReaLchords mixes data, objective, and method changes.

The user study is small (12 participants), reports significance on only two of three questions, and does not appear to correct for multiple comparisons; the qualitative evidence is anecdotal by nature.

The framing conflates diversity collapse with reward hacking in a loose sense; the rule-based repetition penalty itself partially targets the same failure mode, making the exact contribution of the adversarial reward harder to attribute in the full system.

Generalization claims are broader than the evidence: everything is demonstrated on melody-to-chord accompaniment with small 8-layer models; the claim that this is a general mitigation for 'RL post-training of generative sequence models' (e.g., LLMs) is not tested.

strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated problem: diversity collapse from reward hacking in RL post-training, instantiated in a challenging live human-AI music accompaniment setting with a real-time deployed system.

The proposed GAPT method is simple, well-motivated, and grounded in prior adversarial/imitation learning theory (GAIL, GAN stability issues); the two-phase confidence-gated discriminator schedule is a sensible practical solution to the nonstationary-reward problem.

Unusually thorough empirical evaluation: fixed-melody simulation, out-of-distribution (Wikifonia) evaluation, model-model co-adaptation with a learned jamming agent, a user study with 12 expert musicians (IRB-approved, counterbalanced, with paired significance tests), 3 random seeds with variance reporting, and ablations over reward weighting, RL objective (PPO vs. GRPO/Dr.GRPO), discriminator input, and long-sequence behavior.
The user study and qualitative musician feedback directly support the claimed benefits in adaptation speed and perceived agency, going beyond purely automatic metrics.
Commendable reproducibility: code, checkpoints, and datasets are released, and training/hyperparameter details are provided in the appendix.

Honest reporting: the paper acknowledges confounds (e.g., Online MLE appearing strong in model-model interaction, pitch-class count checks in Table 10) and includes negative results in ablations (Exclude Rules leading to degenerate outputs).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea is a GAIL-style discriminator reward added to RL post-training, and the two-phase adaptive update is largely engineering; the paper itself concedes similar ideas exist in AMP (Peng et al., 2021), SeqGAN, and adversarial reward model training (Bukharin et al., 2025). The contribution is primarily an application/integration to a niche domain.

Potential circularity in evaluation: the Vendi Score diversity metric is computed using embeddings from the contrastive reward model, which is also part of the training reward—this biases the evaluation in favor of the method, and the paper does not validate the diversity metric against human judgments.

Missing a key baseline: the paper claims the KL constraint is 'insufficient to mitigate reward hacking' but provides no experiment isolating a KL-only or KL+entropy mitigation strategy; since GAPT differs from the ReaLchords reproduction in several ways (entropy term, dataset mixture, reward ensemble), the attribution of gains to adversarial training alone, versus these other differences, is only partially resolved (the GAPT w/o Adv ablation helps but is not fully clean).

The harmony metric (note-in-chord ratio) is crude, and all learned models remain far below ground truth (0.497 vs. 0.727); additionally, the coherence reward models have weak retrieval performance (R@1 ≈ 0.18), raising questions about the quality of the learned reward signal.
The user study is small (N=12) with only 3 Likert items; only two comparisons reach significance, and conclusions about 'user agency' rest on limited statistical power.

Presentation issues: unresolved citations '(?)' for GRPO/Dr.GRPO in §C.10, an empty 'B.1 Additional Results' section, a hyperlink replacing the chord vocabulary list, Table 6 header says '%' while values are ratios, and the rule-based repetition penalty directly targets the diversity behavior, muddying how much of the diversity gain comes from adversarial training versus explicit penalties.
Hyperparameters of the two-phase schedule (τ=1.0, Kint=5, Twarm=200, window m=3) appear ad hoc, with no sensitivity analysis of the discriminator update schedule itself.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: diversity collapse from coherence-only RL post-training is clearly diagnosed as reward hacking and framed within a real-time human-AI music interaction setting that is genuinely challenging (low latency, no access to partner's future moves).

Comprehensive multi-level evaluation: fixed-melody simulation, model-model co-adaptation with a learned melody agent, out-of-distribution testing on Wikifonia, and an in-person user study with 12 expert musicians including qualitative feedback and IRB documentation.

Substantial ablation studies: random seeds (Table 6), GRPO vs PPO objectives (Table 8), discriminator input ablation (Table 9), reward-weighting ablation (Table 7), long-sequence behavior (Figs. 11-12), and chord-density sanity checks (Table 10).
Transparency and reproducibility: algorithm pseudocode, full hyperparameter details, reward model performance tables, and a stated release of datasets, checkpoints, and code.
Honest reporting of some negative nuances, e.g., Online MLE appearing strongest under a partner trained to accommodate it, and failure modes when rule rewards are removed.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is essentially a GAIL-style adversarial reward (Ho & Ermon, 2016) added to PPO, plus standard GAN stabilization tricks (label smoothing, discriminator freezing/gating). The two-phase schedule is an engineering heuristic rather than a principled or theoretically grounded contribution.

Potential metric circularity: the diversity metric (Vendi Score) uses the chord encoder from the contrastive coherence reward model — the very reward the method claims not to hack. A policy shaped toward that encoder's embedding space could inflate diversity scores without truly diverse musical output; no independent perceptual or musicological diversity validation is provided.

The claim that the KL constraint is insufficient in this setting is asserted but never demonstrated with a direct KL-regularized baseline experiment, weakening the central positioning against standard reward-hacking mitigations.

Absolute gains are modest: harmony improves only marginally over ReaLchords (0.497 vs 0.484 test set) and remains far from ground truth (0.727); diversity still falls well below Online MLE, and the 'restores diversity to near dataset levels' claim in the conclusion overstates the evidence (26.6 vs 27.9 GT on test set, but 11.3 vs 16.4 for Online MLE on OOD).

Small user study (n=12) with three Likert items; p<0.05 significance on only two of three questions, and no correction for multiple comparisons or detailed reporting of effect sizes; some participant quotes (e.g., P6 'I liked the first one better') are weak evidence.

The repetition penalty (a rule forbidding >4 consecutive identical chords) directly targets the observed failure mode, confounding attribution: it is unclear how much of the diversity recovery comes from the adversarial reward versus this hand-crafted penalty, and the ablation in Table 7 does not isolate the repetition penalty alone.

The melody jamming agent is trained with the same adversarial recipe, making model-model results partly self-referential; the Online MLE result in this setting (best harmony) is dismissed rather than analyzed.

Scope is narrow: results are for monophonic melody-to-chord accompaniment on small symbolic datasets; generality of the reward-hacking mitigation claim to 'RL post-training of generative sequence models' (as stated in the abstract) is not supported.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: diversity collapse ('reward hacking') in RL post-training of generative sequence models, instantiated in a demanding real-time interactive music setting.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this domain: fixed-melody simulation, model–model co-adaptation, out-of-distribution evaluation (Wikifonia), a real-time deployment with a user study of 12 expert musicians with IRB approval, and results across 3 random seeds with mean±std reported.

Substantial ablation studies strengthen the claims: reward-weighting ablations (Table 7), robustness of the adversarial reward across RL objectives (PPO vs. GRPO/Dr.GRPO, Table 8), discriminator input ablation (Table 9), and training dynamics analysis (Figures 8–10).

The proposed two-phase, confidence-gated discriminator update schedule is a sensible practical contribution to the known instability of adversarial rewards in RL, and the training dynamics section provides evidence that the discriminator signal is actually being consumed by the critic.
Comparison against the closest prior system (ReaLchords) is direct, including a faithful reproduction and a matched ablation (GAPT w/o Adv.) that isolates the adversarial component.
The paper commits to releasing datasets, checkpoints, training infrastructure, and the real-time interactive system, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Core algorithmic novelty is limited. Rewarding a policy with a discriminator trained on expert data is essentially GAIL (Ho & Ermon, 2016), and combining a discriminator realism reward with a task reward was already done in AMP (Peng et al., 2021). The contribution is largely a reapplication to melody-to-chord accompaniment plus a heuristic two-phase update schedule; the broader significance for reward hacking mitigation beyond this domain is asserted more than demonstrated.

There are confounds in the headline comparison: the ReaLchords reproduction is trained only on Hooktheory while GAPT is trained on three datasets, and GAPT additionally uses an entropy term (γ = 0.01) that the ReaLchords baseline lacks (γ = 0). The improvement over ReaLchords may partly reflect more data and entropy regularization rather than the adversarial reward.

The diversity metric has a circularity concern: the Vendi Score is computed using the chord encoder from the contrastive coherence reward model, the very model family whose reward the adversarially trained policy is optimizing. Improvements on this metric could partially reflect representation drift rather than genuine musical diversity; an independent diversity measure would be more convincing.

Absolute quality remains far from ground truth (harmony 0.497 vs. 0.727 GT), and the margins over baselines are small (e.g., 0.497 vs. 0.484 harmony; Table 1); statistical significance is reported for the user study but not clearly for the simulation results.

The rule-based repetition penalty (no chord repeated more than 4 times) is itself a direct anti-reward-hacking heuristic, so the marginal value of adversarial training over such simple interventions deserves sharper analysis; the reward-weighting ablation (Table 7) shows the rule term is load-bearing.
The user study is small (N=12) and the reward models themselves are weak on test retrieval (R@1 ≈ 0.18), raising questions about the reliability of the coherence reward and reward-based metrics.
Minor presentation issues: empty Appendix B.1, unresolved citations shown as '(?)' for GRPO/Dr.GRPO, and a dangling 'diversity results in Appendix' reference on page 7.
